claims.text: Conventional sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates undergo rapid chemical attack and degradation during long-term exposure to molten aluminum.
A nano-architected engineered coating will protect hot-dip aluminum plating equipment from rapid corrosion by molten aluminum.
The proposed coating will form a stable, self-passivating alumina or similar ceramic layer on the substrate.
A nano-architected coating interface promotes in-situ formation of a stable, self-healing inert oxide layer.
Hot-dip aluminum plating equipment is continuously exposed to molten aluminum at approximately 700–800°C.
A protective alumina scale can act as an effective diffusion barrier.
The nano-architected interface will sustain a protective oxide scale during exposure to molten aluminum.
Exposure of the coating to molten aluminum causes formation of a passivating ceramic layer.
The ceramic layer limits direct chemical contact between molten aluminum and the underlying metal.
A continuous, self-healing oxide barrier reduces further corrosion and substrate degradation.
Coated components will have lower corrosion rates than uncoated components under the same hot-dip aluminum conditions.
Coated components will have longer service lives than uncoated components.
Uncoated conventional metal parts quickly deteriorate under continuous contact with molten aluminum.
The protective effect is expected to remain valid within the temperature and aluminum chemistry typical of hot-dip plating.
Mechanical stress, thermal cycling, and poor coating adhesion may limit the protective effect.
The degree of service-life and corrosion-resistance improvement depends on coating adhesion, coating thickness, and maintenance of a continuous oxide scale.
